editorial:
Imagine meeting someone from the other side of the world who shared your wildest dreams and your biggest mistakes. That is exactly what happens here. You get to follow two women, Inge from Germany and Maria from Uruguay, who both joined radical groups in the 60s to try and change the world. They ended up in exile, far from home, and eventually meet in Cuba. The vibe is very personal and honest. It feels less like a history lesson and more like a deep conversation between two old friends who have seen the worst and best of humanity. 

What really works is how the film avoids taking sides. It does not try to make them heroes or villains; it just shows them as people. The pacing is slow and thoughtful, which lets you really feel their emotions. If you like stories about politics, rebellion, and the human spirit, you will love this. Since it is an older documentary, you might want to track down the 4K Blu-ray for your physical collection to get the best picture, or look for it as a high-def rental on Apple TV to see every detail of their expressions.
endingExplained: The movie wraps up by showing these two women reflecting on their lives while staying in Cuba. They realize that while their revolutions did not work out the way they planned, their struggle gave their lives meaning. The final scenes show them accepting their roles as outsiders. They find a kind of peace in their shared friendship, proving that even when big political dreams fail, human connection is what actually saves you in the end.
targetAudience: Ideal for anyone who loves real life stories about rebels and history.
